topics.title: Whole numbers to 100,000
topics.summary: Place value, reading and comparing large numbers.

steps.text: Base-ten blocks: a flat is 100, a rod is 10, a cube is 1. This shows 243.

Each place is 10 times the place on its right:
ones → tens → hundreds → thousands → ten thousands.
In 47,352 the 4 is in the ten thousands place, so it stands for 40,000.

interact.prompt: In 47,352, what value does the 7 stand for?
interact.explain: The 7 is in the thousands place: 7,000.

steps.text:
Line the numbers up by place value:
38,415
38,154
Start from the left. 3 = 3, 8 = 8, then 4 > 1. The first place that differs decides.

interact.explain: In the hundreds, 4 is greater than 1.

steps.text: Column addition: add each place, starting from the ones. Carry when a place makes 10 or more.
Column subtraction: when the top digit is too small, rename 1 from the next place.

questions.hint: You need to rename across the zero: 6,302 = 62 hundreds + 10 tens… take it one place at a time.
Think 8,999 + 1. Subtract from 8,999 first, then add 1.

topics.title: Factors and multiples
topics.summary: Find factors and multiples of whole numbers.

steps.text: Arrange 12 counters in equal rows. 3 rows of 4 works, so 3 and 4 are factors of 12.

interact.prompt: Which number is a factor of 12?

steps.text: Skip counting turns a times table into jumps on a number line.
Use facts you know: 7 × 8 = 7 × 4 × 2 = 28 × 2 = 56.
Your turn: 6 × 8.
Think of 243 × 3 as 3 groups of 243 blocks. Split by place value and multiply each part.
Your turn: 125 × 4.
Split the 2-digit number into tens and ones, multiply each, then add.
Your turn: 52 × 13.
Share 84 counters into 4 equal groups. Share the tens first, then the ones.
Your turn: 96 ÷ 3.
Share 17 sweets among 5 children. Each gets 3, and 2 are left over.
The remainder is what is left after sharing equally.
Your turn: 47 ÷ 6.

topics.title: Fractions
topics.summary: Equivalent fractions, and adding and subtracting fractions.

steps.text: Fold a strip of paper in half and shade one half.
Cut each part into smaller equal parts. The shaded amount stays the same.
Your turn: 2/3 = ?/9.
When the parts are the same size, add or subtract the tops and keep the bottom.
Your turn: 5/9 − 2/9.
In practice, type the top and bottom numbers in the two boxes.

topics.title: Decimals
topics.summary: Tenths, and adding and subtracting decimals.

steps.text: Cut a whole into 10 equal parts. Each part is one tenth, 0.1. Three parts are 0.3.
2 and 4 tenths is written 2.4. Line up the decimal points to add: 2.4 + 1.5 = 3.9.

interact.explain: Tenths are the first place after the point.

topics.title: Length, mass and volume
topics.summary: Change between km and m, m and cm, kg and g, ℓ and ml, and add measures.

steps.text: A metre stick is 100 cm long. So 1 m = 100 cm. In the same way, 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 ℓ = 1,000 ml.
2 m 35 cm is 2 metre sticks and 35 cm more: 200 + 35 = 235 cm.
To go the other way, take out the whole units first: 3,450 g = 3 kg 450 g.
Your turn: 4 ℓ 250 ml = ? ml.
To add 1 kg 600 g and 2 kg 750 g, change both into grams first, then add.
Your turn: 3 m 40 cm + 1 m 85 cm = ? cm.

topics.title: Money
topics.summary: Add prices and give change in dollars and cents.

steps.text: 100 cents make 1 dollar. $3.45 is 3 dollars and 45 cents.
Add the dollars, then the cents. Change 100¢ into $1 when you can.
Shopkeepers count up to give change: from the price to the next dollar, then to the note.
Your turn: a book costs $12.40. You pay with $20.

topics.title: Time
topics.summary: Read clocks, use the 24-hour clock, and work out how long things take.

steps.text: The short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows the minutes. Each number on the clock is 5 minutes for the long hand.
Read the hour hand first, then count the minutes in 5s.
Your turn.
A day has 24 hours. The 24-hour clock does not start again at noon: 1 p.m. is 13:00, 6 p.m. is 18:00. Midnight is 00:00.
For p.m. times, take 12 away from the hour.
Your turn: 7:15 p.m. in 24-hour time.
Draw a timeline. Jump to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then the minutes left. Add the jumps.
To find an end time, add the hours first, then the minutes.
Your turn: from 8:50 a.m. to 10:15 a.m.

topics.title: Angles, area and symmetry
topics.summary: Kinds of angles and turns, perimeter and area of rectangles, and lines of symmetry.

steps.text: Fold a paper twice to make a square corner. That is a right angle, 90°.
Put your square corner on an angle. Smaller is acute. Bigger is obtuse.
Each 1/4 turn is a right angle. A full turn is 4 right angles, 360°.
Your turn: what kind of angle is this?
Walk around the edge of a shape: that distance is the perimeter. Cover it with 1 cm squares: the number of squares is the area.
Perimeter: add all the sides.
Area: rows × squares in each row.
Your turn: the area of a 9 cm by 5 cm rectangle.
Fold a paper heart down the middle. The two halves match exactly, so the fold is a line of symmetry.
A rectangle's diagonal is NOT a line of symmetry. Fold it and see.
Your turn: how many lines of symmetry does a square have?

topics.title: Tables and graphs
topics.summary: Read bar graphs and tables, and compare and add what they show.

steps.text: Check the scale first. Then go across from the top of a bar to the scale to read it.
To compare, read both bars, then subtract.
Your turn: how many books altogether?

topics.title: Word problems with bar models
topics.summary: Draw a bar model, then solve.

steps.text: Ana has 1,250 stickers. Ben has 860. How many altogether? Watch how to draw it.
Your turn: Ana and Ben have 3,000 stickers altogether. Ana has 1,800. How many does Ben have?
Raj has 340 cards. Mei has 125 more than Raj. How many does Mei have? Watch the two bars.
Your turn: Mei has 820 cards. Raj has 560. How many more does Mei have?
Lea has 3 times as many shells as Jun. Jun has 24. How many do they have altogether? Draw units!
Your turn: Siti has 5 times as many marbles as Tomas. Tomas has 15. How many does Siti have?
